change.name: Change: Rate, Accumulation, and Flow
change.truth: A value, a local rate and an accumulated total retain different things. Repeated updates can make the next address depend on the path already taken.
change.qfep_connection: Calculus vocabulary for later research: distinguish local change, finite accumulation and retained history. The encounters support these comparisons; they do not measure a QFEP term or entropy threshold.
change.formula: rate = rise / h; total += f(x) * width; position += direction(position, time) * speed * delta
change.demonstration: Compare a wide finite difference with an analytic local rate. Keep the function fixed while changing the samples used for an area estimate. Predict the net height difference of an arch, then compare it with a finite sum of its signed rate. Let each particle update determine the address of its next direction lookup.
change.description: Two halls build from addresses and sampling: value versus local rate; contribution versus total; signed accumulation versus endpoint difference; then trajectories in a direction field. Each comparison makes a limit of its representation inspectable before Forces introduces velocity, acceleration and carried motion.
learning_objectives: Write a finite-rate function over a nonzero horizontal interval, with the independent variable and units stated
On a separate lesson, accumulate height-times-width samples of the same supplied smooth function
Vary count or sample position independently; distinguish finite reference sums from exact integrals
Use the different bridge arch as a signed-change comparison; separate net change from total travel
Sample a supplied direction field at the position produced by the previous update
Distinguish unit direction, speed, elapsed seconds and displacement in the declared canvas frame
Inspect field time, particle updates and misleading trail joins at wraps without claiming an unimplemented repair
On a return, compare one step with two half-steps under identical start, field, speed and duration; distinguish this from changing SPEED
Prepare Forces by distinguishing an immediately prescribed velocity from velocity retained and changed by acceleration

curation_history.truth: Things change. Change accumulates. Accumulation flows.
curation_history.qfep_connection: Foundation â€” the calculus substrate. Derivative as instantaneous rate of change, integral as accumulated quantity, vector field as flow. The conceptual vocabulary that forces, wavefunctions, randomness, and noise will all use.
curation_history.demonstration: Watch a tangent line slide along a curve and read its slope. Pump up the count on a Riemann sum and watch rectangles converge into a continuous integral. Release particles into a vector field and watch them flow. Take over the catalyst and sustain its contact on a target â€” accumulation made bracelet-felt.
curation_history.description: The calculus substrate, made visible. Change as instantaneous rate (derivative); accumulation as continuous addition (integral); vector field as flow at every point in space. This sequence's job is to establish the vocabulary so forces, wavefunctions, randomness, and noise can name what they're doing instead of running on an unintroduced backbone.
learning_objectives: Change as instantaneous rate: the derivative; slope of a curve at a point; velocity as rate of position
Slope across a curve: how slope itself becomes a function (derivative-as-function)
Accumulation as continuous addition: the integral; area under a curve; total from rate
Riemann sum: discrete accumulation approaching continuous; how rectangles become integrals in the limit
Vector fields: change-and-flow at every point in space; the first encounter with a function of space (not just time)
The fundamental theorem of calculus: change and accumulation are inverse operations; one undoes the other
Carry-forward to forces and waves: F = ma is calculus made physical; sine is the function whose second derivative is itself negated
